news.2026-10-17-petrole-110-dollars-ormu: Oil is back at $110: Hormuz flares up and Ukraine's "energy truce" falls apart
Brent crude touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May. Ships are being attacked around Hormuz, and Kyiv has resumed strikes on Russian refineries.
Brent touched $110 during the session, a level not seen since May, before closing at $109.86 (+3.7%). US WTI crude finished at $101.41 [1].

At least nine tankers and cargo ships have been attacked around Hormuz since Sunday. US Central Command says Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday. According to Kpler, 9.4 million barrels a day passed through the strait last week, about 70% of the pre-war level [1].

The energy truce announced by Donald Trump has collapsed: Volodymyr Zelensky says he resumed strikes on Russian refineries because Moscow did not respect the ceasefire. Trump called the decision a "disgrace". A drone attack reportedly halted the main unit at the Ryazan refinery [1].

Two sources of supply are hit at the same time: Gulf oil, which passes through an increasingly risky strait, and Russian oil and refined products, targeted by Ukrainian drones. When supply is in doubt, prices rise fast [1].
This also shows how fragile "truces" announced without details are: the energy one lasted only a few days [1].
A more expensive barrel is paid for at the pump and on your heating bill, with a short delay. If the price stays around $110, petrol and diesel could rise again in the coming weeks.

news.2026-10-17-chili-bolivie-visite-kas: Chile and Bolivia are talking again: first state visit in 71 years, but still no sea access
Chilean President José Antonio Kast is in La Paz. The two countries, estranged since 1978, are signing deals on mining, electricity and the border, but not on access to the sea.

Chilean President José Antonio Kast made the first state visit by a Chilean leader to Bolivia in 71 years, in La Paz. The two countries broke off diplomatic relations in 1978 and did not announce the return of ambassadors [1][2].

Ministers signed agreements on mining integration, electricity interconnection, corridors linking the Atlantic to the Pacific, border security and the status of Bolivians living in Chile. The two countries will also negotiate an update to a trade agreement [1][2].

Sovereign access to the sea, which Bolivia lost at the International Court of Justice in 2018, was not on the agenda. President Rodrigo Paz recalled that this claim is written into Bolivia's Constitution, while saying the past must not hold back development [1][3].

Landlocked since the War of the Pacific (1879-1884), Bolivia sends about 70% of its foreign trade through ports in northern Chile. Normalising relations therefore means first of all making that transit easier [3].

Officials also discussed putting the Arica–La Paz railway back into service, provided for by the 1904 treaty, and a border crossing open 24 hours a day at Tambo Quemado–Chungará [1]. Kast invited Paz to Chile in 2027 [1].

It doesn't affect your daily life, but it is a good example of a simple idea: two neighbours, at odds for almost fifty years, are starting to trade again because their economic interests outweigh the historical quarrel.

news.2026-10-17-indonesie-bourse-msci.ti: Indonesia's stock market loses almost 12% in one day, its worst fall since 1998
news.2026-10-17-indonesie-bourse-msci.su: The MSCI index provider is considering demoting Indonesia out of the emerging-markets club. The Jakarta stock market collapsed on Friday.
news.2026-10-17-indonesie-bourse-msci.po: The Jakarta stock index lost 11.57% on Friday and ended at 5,185 points, its lowest level of the year. Bloomberg reports the biggest one-session fall since January 1998 [1][2].

Index provider MSCI opened a consultation on Thursday on a possible move of Indonesia from emerging-market status to "standalone market" status. It cites a lack of transparency about who owns the shares and suspicions of coordinated trading [1][2].
It is not the first warning of the year: at the end of January, a similar MSCI warning had already cost the stock market about 12% and more than $80 billion in value in about a week [3].
news.2026-10-17-indonesie-bourse-msci.wh: MSCI builds indices that very large funds follow. When a country is dropped or demoted, those funds may have to sell its shares, which explains investors' panic.
No decision has been made: it is only a consultation, but the mere threat is enough to make the market fall [1][2].
news.2026-10-17-indonesie-bourse-msci.fo: You are probably not affected directly. It is mostly a reminder that foreign investors' confidence in a stock market can evaporate in a single day when its rules or transparency are questioned.

news.2026-10-17-armenie-onu-guterres-rou: Armenia: the UN chief in Yerevan, a road across the country to link Azerbaijan to its exclave, and a peace treaty still unsigned
Antonio Guterres meets Prime Minister Pashinyan during a UN summit on nature. Peace with Azerbaijan and the TRIPP road project are on the agenda.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is in Yerevan for the COP17 leaders' summit, the UN biodiversity conference. On Thursday he met Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan; he is the second UN chief to visit Armenia [1][2].

The peace treaty with Azerbaijan, initialled in Washington in August 2025, is still not signed. Baku demands changes to Armenia's Constitution, and Armenian prisoners are still held in Azerbaijan [3].

The two men also discussed TRIPP, a road and infrastructure that would link Azerbaijan to its Nakhchivan exclave by crossing southern Armenia. A US-Armenian agreement provides for a company to build them, and engineering surveys have begun [2][3].
Armenia has no access to the sea. A road crossing its south could change the region's transport map, which is why this project is closely watched [3].

On the sidelines of the summit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met Georgia's prime minister and called for a timetable for closer cooperation. Tbilisi had cut its air links with Iran after US sanctions on Iranian airlines [4].

A lasting peace in the Caucasus would make the routes between Central Asia, Turkey and Europe safer, and so make the goods and energy that use them more reliable. You won't see it in your daily life, but it is one of the projects redrawing Eurasian trade.

news.2026-10-17-kenya-ebola-deuxieme-cas: Ebola reaches Kenya: second case confirmed in a relative of the first patient
A 39-year-old man, already in isolation, has tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus. Authorities say there is no transmission in the general population.
Kenya's Health Ministry confirmed a second Ebola case on 14 October: a 39-year-old man, a relative of the first patient, who fell ill on 13 October while already in quarantine [1][2].
Two laboratories, including KEMRI-CDC, each confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. The first patient, a 40-year-old Kenyan, died on 5 October in Nairobi [1][2].
Of 128 contacts identified, 113 had been traced, including 108 in quarantine in Kenya. The ministry says the two cases are linked and that there is no evidence of wider transmission [1][2].

Kenya is affected by an outbreak coming from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where most cases are concentrated. The organisation CARE describes it as the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, with more than 9,000 cases [3].
Spotting and isolating contacts very quickly, as Kenya is doing, is what helps limit the spread [1][2].
The risk to you is very low: the Kenyan cases are being tracked and isolated. But an outbreak in a large East African country can weigh on tourism, flights and regional trade.

news.2026-10-17-tanzanie-gaz-42-milliard: Tanzania: the country's biggest gas project, $42 billion, is still waiting to be signed
The finance minister says a deal with Shell and Equinor is close, but it was due to be signed before June and still isn't.
Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar said on 13 October that Tanzania was close to an agreement on its $42 billion liquefied natural gas (LNG) project. The final agreements have not been signed [1].
The goal of signing before June 2026 was missed. A special law on LNG investment could be ready by the end of 2026, according to a deputy minister cited by bne IntelliNews [1].
The project targets 47.13 trillion cubic feet of gas. Equinor and Shell lead it, with ExxonMobil, Pavilion Energy, Medco Energi and the state company TPDC [2].
At $42 billion, it is the biggest investment ever considered in the country, which explains why the government wants a dedicated legal framework before signing [2].
Production would only start about eight years after signing: the economic effect therefore plays out over the long term [2].
A project this size won't show up at the pump for years. But it shows why East Africa attracts energy giants, and why their negotiations with states take so long.

news.2026-10-17-yemen-houthis-mer-rouge-: Yemen: the Houthis strike the government's palace in Aden, and the Security Council is alarmed for the Red Sea
After taking the port of Mocha last month, the rebels are attacking the city where the government sits. The UN condemns attacks on airports, energy and shipping.

On Thursday, an attack on the Al-Maashiq palace in Aden left 5 dead and 16 injured, according to Yemen's health minister. Houthi-aligned media say they targeted the operations headquarters, run by Saudi officers [2].

The Houthis took the port of Mocha on 10 September, then the island of Perim the next day, on the edge of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. The government speaks of a "tactical withdrawal"; Yemeni media have since said they retook it, which the Houthis deny and which we could not verify [3].
The UN Security Council on 15 October condemned Houthi attacks on civilians, airports and energy facilities, as well as threats to shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb strait [4].
Bab-el-Mandeb is the southern gate of the Red Sea: ships heading for the Suez Canal pass through it. Whoever holds the coast can threaten the passage [3][4].
The Yemen war is mixing with the Gulf war: Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of arming and training the Houthis [2].
If ships avoid the Red Sea, they go around Africa: longer and more expensive. That can raise the price of some goods from Asia and of fuel transport.

news.2026-10-17-singapour-brume-poursuit: Toxic haze: Singapore threatens to prosecute the companies behind the Indonesian fires
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong says he is looking into which companies are responsible and mentions prosecutions. The air is the most polluted of the year.

In a post on Thursday evening, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore was looking into which companies might be responsible for the forest and peatland fires in Indonesia, and could act under its transboundary pollution law [1][2].

The pollution index in the centre of the island reached as high as 229 on Friday, the highest this year. Singapore has had 12 days in a row of unhealthy air since 5 October, its longest streak since the 2015 crisis [3].
Indonesia accepts foreign help, approved by President Prabowo Subianto. Four people died on Java fighting the fires [1][4].
Prosecuting companies for smoke that crosses borders is difficult: investigations depend on the cooperation of foreign authorities, legal experts warn [1].
The Singapore government has also sped up the distribution of N95 masks to the public, a sign that the situation is being taken seriously [3].

If you travel or work in South-East Asia, the haze can weigh on health and daily life: the air in Singapore has been unhealthy for nearly two weeks. It is also a test of whether companies can be held responsible for fires that pollute other countries.

news.2026-10-17-chine-ue-hybrides-terres: China agrees to sell half as many hybrid cars to Europe, and promises a "fast lane" for rare earths
After two days of negotiations in Beijing, the EU announces an agreement in principle on hybrids. Beijing says rare earths will keep arriving in Europe.

European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced on 9 October that China would cut its hybrid car exports to the EU, after two days of talks in Beijing with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. It covers both conventional and plug-in hybrids [1][2].

The "half" is calculated against forecast sales, not current sales. According to Šefčovič, it would keep several million Chinese vehicles out of the EU over four years compared with a no-deal scenario. The mechanism (quotas or carmaker commitments) is not specified, and the deal still has to be approved by the EU [2].

According to CNBC, China said on 15 October that it remained ready to ease, through a "green channel", export licences for rare earths and magnets to Europe, even as the deadline of the trade deal with the United States approaches. In return it asks the EU to support some of its exports in dual-use sectors [3].
For Europe, the deal would limit the arrival of Chinese vehicles while saving it on tariffs [2].
Sources differ on what has actually been secured: the tariff savings are put at different figures depending on the outlet, and Beijing has not promised rare-earth licence volumes [2][3].
If you are looking for a hybrid car, the choice of Chinese models could shrink. Rare earths, for their part, go into the magnets of electric cars, wind turbines and many devices.
